cards.title: Choose an SMS platform: consolidate with email, then price-shop
cards.summary: Pick SMS in the same platform as your email for management simplicity, but get competing quotes since SMS pricing varies and features rarely matter.
cards.use_when: Selecting or renegotiating the SMS/text platform for your store's lifecycle messaging.
steps: Prioritize running SMS inside the same platform as your email (e.g., Klaviyo, Omnisend, Attentive) so lists, segments and reporting live in one place.
Because consolidation often costs more, request a quote from your current email provider for their SMS add-on.
Take that quote to the main SMS competitors (source names Attentive and Postscript as the 'big dogs'; others such as OneText exist) and ask them to beat it, letting them compete on price.

Decide mainly on price and ease of management. The source argues the platforms' differentiating AI features are unlikely to be used and 'the basics will drive 99% of your revenue,' so don't agonize over the choice.
caveats: This is the presenter's opinion (Max / Well Copy); platform pricing and feature sets change, so verify current quotes and contracts.
Platform names and capabilities are source-specific and may be outdated.

cards.title: Capture phone numbers in your popup from day one
cards.summary: Add an SMS phone field to your email popup now, even with no SMS program, so your text list compounds instead of starting from zero later.
cards.use_when: Designing or revising the email/SMS signup popup that captures subscribers at store entry.
steps: Include a phone-number field in your popup even if you have no SMS list yet. The source's argument: if you start collecting SMS today and only decide to use it a year later, you already have a large list to market to; if you wait, you have zero.

Use a popup tool optimized for SMS capture. The source recommends Alia (allpopups.com) over native platform popups, reporting native Klaviyo opt-ins around 3–4% vs. Alia submit rates around 9% and typically ~16% when the offer is strong.
Track phone opt-in rate as a headline metric; the source frames getting ~60% of ad traffic to hand over a phone number as a major cheap-conversion unlock.
Refresh offers/tests over time so capture rate is judged on its own, not against one weak offer.
caveats: Opt-in rates cited (3–4%, 9%, ~16%) are the presenter's observed figures for specific brands, not guaranteed benchmarks.
Tool names and interface details may change; verify current setup.

cards.title: Use a quiz popup and 'activate your discount' copy to lift phone capture
cards.summary: Lead with a micro-quiz before asking for contact info, and phrase the SMS ask as finishing the signup they already started.
cards.use_when: Building the SMS/phone opt-in step of your store popup to raise subscriber capture rate.
steps: Start the popup with a quiz or micro-commitment (source: 'this is what works') before requesting email or phone — engage the visitor first, then ask.
Choose a template that offers a discount (e.g., 10% off) and asks a qualifying question, then transitions to the contact step.
Change the button label from 'Continue' (which signals another required step) to 'Claim now' to reduce drop-off.

Replace generic SMS copy like 'Sign up for texts' or 'Get exclusive deals' with action-oriented continuity copy such as 'Finish signing up with text to activate your discount' — the visitor has already given email and wants the discount activated.
Do not stack an extra discount for SMS. The source reports no marginal impact from offering extra % off for the phone number.
caveats: Quiz-first flows and copy results are the presenter's experience, not a universal rule.
Source claims 15%+ opt-in is achievable but notes most forms they review sit at 5–6% submit rate.

cards.title: Treat SMS as high-urgency, low-frequency — not a nurture channel
cards.summary: SMS tolerates far fewer sends than email; reserve it for time-sensitive, worth-the-ding messages or you get punishing unsubscribe rates.
cards.use_when: Deciding what content belongs in SMS blasts vs. email, and setting the tone of your text program.
steps: Recognize the cost of intrusion: source reports SMS unsubscribe rates of 3–5% vs. roughly 0.3% for email, because a text is a phone ding the customer notices.
Send far less on SMS than on email. Cut nurture content (testimonials, brand storytelling, evergreen best-sellers) — the source says it 'doesn't work' on SMS and drives unsubscribes long-term.
Reserve SMS for high-urgency events: product launches, back-in-stock/restock alerts, flash sales, private events, insider details.
Make each text 'worth receiving' and get straight to the point; test whether a timely-urgency angle (e.g., 'selling fast this week') outperforms a generic nurture angle before scaling frequency.
caveats: Unsubscribe-rate comparison is the presenter's cited figure, not a site metric.
Source explicitly says this is a starting point; some brands they run send daily because it fits their context.

cards.title: Keep texts under 160 characters and cost-control emojis and images
cards.summary: Message length, emojis and images directly drive SMS cost, so measure credits and let cost inform creative choices.
cards.use_when: Writing and budgeting SMS campaign and flow messages, especially for large lists.
steps: Keep messages under 160 characters. Going to 161 characters can make it a multi-segment send billed as two SMS, roughly doubling cost.
Limit emojis: one emoji can consume ~60–70 characters of the SMS budget, eating your character allowance.
Understand images: adding any image converts an SMS into an MMS, which the source says costs roughly three times more.
Apply the same discipline to longer messages generally — every extra character can push you into extra billed credits.
Check your platform's credit/character accounting and current pricing, since these figures are source-specific.
caveats: Character-to-cost and MMS pricing figures (e.g., ~1.5 cents/send, ~3x MMS) are illustrative and vary by platform, plan and country.
Verify current interface and billing rules before relying on exact thresholds.

cards.title: Test SMS vs. MMS images on net profit, not revenue
cards.summary: Image (MMS) messages can lift revenue and buyer intent but cost ~3x, so decide by net profit after send cost, not top-line revenue.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to include product images in SMS campaigns or abandonment flows.
steps: Run A/B tests of identical messages with and without an image, and track revenue AND send cost for each version.
Source example: the image version generated ~1.3x more revenue but cost 3x to send — worse ROI on revenue, yet net-profit-positive once the extra revenue ($1,300 back on $200 extra spend) is counted.
Source example 2: no-image message did $620 revenue vs. $1,200 with image; the image cost only ~$15 more at low volume, so it was a clear win — showing results depend on list size and offer.
Note the behavioral pattern: image messages often get lower click-through (people see the product and click with higher intent), but can produce more revenue.

Use images deliberately for high-impact moments only (new flavor/product drop, key abandoned-cart/welcome messages). The source notes a 9-figure brand (Grain's) rarely uses images, reserving them for important sends.
caveats: Both examples are low-volume/single-brand results, explicitly not guarantees; the source warns it 'doesn't always play out this way.'
Retest on your own offers and list size, since cost scales with list size.

cards.title: Build the five core SMS flows (welcome + four abandonments + post-purchase)
cards.summary: Every brand should run a welcome flow, site/browse/cart/checkout abandonment, and a post-purchase replenishment or win-back flow.
cards.use_when: Setting up or auditing the automated (flow) side of an SMS program.
steps: Welcome flow: triggered when someone joins via the popup (often with a discount). Keep it simple — introduce the brand and drive the discount.

Four abandonment flows, kept dead simple: site abandoned (browsed site, no product page), browse abandoned (viewed a product page), cart abandoned (added to cart), checkout abandoned (reached checkout).
Post-purchase / replenishment / win-back flow: bring buyers back after their first order.
Keep abandonment messages single and simple (see the US compliance card) and split by new vs. returning buyers when you can.

Treat these basics as the moneymakers: the source reports one brand's core flows producing $517k, with $293k from welcome, $107k cart abandoned, $46k browse abandoned, $20k retention, and $13k site abandoned in a month.
caveats: Revenue figures are a single agency portfolio example, not a benchmark to expect.
Exact flow structure should be adjusted per brand context.

cards.title: Structure the SMS welcome flow: day 1, day 3, day 5
cards.summary: Send a tight three-message SMS welcome — intro with discount, educational reminder, then last-chance — inside a short window while subscribers are warm.
cards.use_when: Writing the SMS welcome series triggered by your popup signup.
steps: Send SMS 1 immediately: give the discount with no preamble (the person just signed up for it).
Send SMS 2 about 2 days later (day 3) with a bit of brand/differentiation info or a reminder of the discount.
Send SMS 3 on about day 5 as an 'absolute last chance' before the code expires.
Keep the window tight — do not delay sends by weeks; hit people while they're warm.

The more aggressive alternative (source cites Grain's) is a message every single day with the discount repeated, mixing in educational messages; the source frames both as valid but prefers the tighter three-message structure.
If doubling up, keep messages short: e.g., 'Welcome to [brand], here's 20% off, code WELCOME20, shop now,' then a last-chance text days later. A/B test images and delay timing.
caveats: Dense cadence (e.g., daily) should be tempered by your audience and follows compliance/consent rules.
Delay timings are recommendations, not tested universals.

cards.title: Send only one SMS per abandonment event (US compliance)
cards.summary: US rules limit abandonment flows to a single SMS per recipient within 48 hours, so keep cart/browse/checkout texts to one simple message.
cards.use_when: Setting up SMS cart, browse, site, or checkout abandonment flows, especially for US customers.
steps: Build each abandonment flow to send exactly one SMS per recipient — the source states sending more than one SMS in an abandonment flow is illegal in the US.
Schedule that single message to fire within 48 hours of the triggering event (source cites Klaviyo's built-in constraint of one SMS per recipient in cart abandonment within 48 hours).
Confirm the recipient has SMS consent before the flow sends.

Because you get one shot, make it simple: browse abandoned → 'Eyes on something? You have good taste. Keep shopping' (fire ~60 min after browse); cart/checkout → 'Looks like you forgot something — finish your order.'
Optionally test adding an MMS product image against plain text, and split buy-intent: give non-buyers a welcome discount code (e.g., 'use WILDWELCOME20') while keeping buyers' messages simpler.
Verify current carrier/platform compliance rules, which can change.
caveats: 48-hour/one-message rule is described for the US; other jurisdictions differ.
The source says this is a compliance ceiling, not a ceiling on how creative the single message can be.

cards.title: Time post-purchase and replenishment SMS to the buy cycle
cards.summary: Send a cross-sell/upsell SMS about 10–14 days after delivery and a replenishment reminder just before the product runs out.
cards.use_when: Building the post-purchase and replenishment SMS flow for your store.
steps: Send SMS 1 around day 10–14 after order delivery, while the buyer is in the honeymoon phase: ask if they're enjoying the product and suggest cross-sell/upsell or a repeat purchase.

For consumable/replenishment products, add SMS 2 timed to when the product runs out. Calculate it: e.g., Athletic Greens — 30-day supply plus 7-day delivery → send on ~day 35, 'are you running low? reorder.'
Hold offers initially; the source recommends not adding discounts to these early post-purchase messages until later.
Don't over-send: remember buyers also receive your campaign blasts, so two well-timed post-purchase messages are usually enough.
Consider keeping all win-back-style post-purchase messages in one flow triggered on order placement.
caveats: The source says this flow varies so much brand-to-brand that no single verified template applies; the athletic-greens math is an illustration.
Replenishment timing depends on your own product consumption and delivery cycle.

cards.title: Trigger SMS win-back at double the average time between purchases
cards.summary: Use 2x the customer's average reorder interval as the win-back trigger, then send a short 72-hour flash offer plus a last-chance reminder.
cards.use_when: Setting the trigger point and offer structure for an SMS win-back flow for lapsed buyers.
steps: Estimate average time between purchases for your store (e.g., 45 days) and multiply by two (→ ~90 days you'd likely consider a customer lapsed).
At that trigger, send SMS 1 with a flash offer, e.g., 'We miss you — here's 30% off, exclusive code, expires in 72 hours.'
Wait ~2 days and send SMS 2 as a last-chance/expiry reminder.
Keep it to roughly two messages; the source says these two plus your post-purchase sends are all you need before the cycle repeats.
Confirm your estimate with actual reorder-interval data rather than guessing.
caveats: '2x average time between purchases' is a source heuristic, not a universal law.
Offer depth (e.g., 30%) is an example; test margin impact before adopting.

cards.title: Cap SMS blasts at about two campaigns per week for most brands
cards.summary: Baseline around two SMS campaigns weekly, reserving higher frequency for launch-heavy or aggressive-acquisition brands with big lists.
cards.use_when: Setting the SMS campaign (blast) calendar and frequency for your store.
steps: Start with a baseline of about two SMS campaigns per week for a typical brand. Send at least one per week at minimum.
For aggressive-acquisition brands spending heavily (source cites Grain's), sending an SMS every single day to people who've never bought is acceptable if you have a large list and lots of news.
Ease off for existing buyers: for one-time-purchase or subscription brands, reduce frequency to buyers, and the source says don't text active subscribers at all.
During major sale pushes you can increase to daily or even two-a-day (source references a 9-figure brand's calendar), then return to baseline after the push.
Don't force sends: the source prefers saving SMS for big announcements to avoid unsubscribes — 'do not force out SMS if you don't have to.'
caveats: Frequency recommendations are the presenter's opinion and depend on list size, brand news and consent.
Buyer-vs-non-buyer cuts are specific to a sub/large-brand context.

cards.title: Plan an SMS campaign calendar around high-urgency events
cards.summary: Fill the SMS calendar with launches, restocks, time-boxed sales and timely trend/drop alerts — not evergreen nurture.
cards.use_when: Building the monthly SMS campaign calendar and choosing which messages to send.
steps: Anchor sends to genuinely urgent, timely events: product launches, back-in-stock/restock alerts, flash sales, private events, insider news, and time-boxed 'selling fast this week' trend alerts.
For a launch, send the announcement, then a reminder a couple days later (source example: sent on the 4th, reminder on the 6th).
Use SMS-exclusive flash sales — the source highlights exclusive-to-list offers as especially effective.

You can relabel messages with urgency even when literal urgency is absent (e.g., frame a past collection as a 'restock,' or a product as 'running low') because restocks perform well — but note the source's caution that non-urgent nurture performed worst and drove more unsubscribes.

Example: a brand sent just five SMS in a month (pre-order collection, list-exclusive free-item offer, framed restock, reminder, launch) and reports >$100k and 16% of total store revenue — showing a lean, intentional calendar can perform.
caveats: This revenue example is a single case, not a benchmark.
Framing messages as 'restock' or 'running low' when untrue is the source's tactic; consider trust and advertising-standards implications before using.

cards.title: Broadcast SMS to the full list with a tight exclusion list
cards.summary: Default to sending SMS to all subscribers and only suppress chronically unengaged numbers, cleaning monthly — deep engagement segmentation leaves money on the table.
cards.use_when: Segmenting your SMS list for campaign sends and deciding send exclusions.
steps: Send to all SMS subscribers rather than narrow engaged segments. The source notes people who never click a text still purchase (they see the message and go to the site directly).
Maintain a simple exclusion list: exclude a contact only after they've received ~15 texts with zero clicks ever.
Also exclude anyone you've bought from in ways that make them a poor target (e.g., don't text active subscribers on a subscription).
Clean the list about monthly to control cost, since SMS is expensive per send.
For big announcements (e.g., a New Year's Eve sale), send to the entire list with no exclusions.
Don't 'get too cute' building engaged segments — the source reports broadcasting usually makes the most money.
caveats: '15 texts with zero clicks' is a source heuristic, not a tested threshold.
Platform automation may handle exclusion lists differently; verify your setup.

cards.title: Test delays, offers and images before scaling SMS
cards.summary: Validate timing, offer and image choices with A/B tests and your own brand context rather than copying a template wholesale.
cards.use_when: Deciding what to change or expand once your core SMS flows and campaigns are running.
steps: Test message timing/delays (welcome day spacing, abandonment send windows, win-back trigger).
Test offers: whether a discount changes behavior, and how deep, before adding them to flows (source found no marginal lift from extra SMS discounts).
A/B test including images versus not in flows and campaigns, tracking net profit (revenue minus send cost) rather than revenue alone.
Keep the tests attached to the core flows the source says drive most revenue; add complexity only after the basics are measured.
Expect results to be brand-specific: the source explicitly says this isn't a copy-exactly recipe and cites running daily SMS or intricate flows for some brands.
caveats: Source advises treating its structure as a starting point, not scripture; verify with your own data.
Small-sample tests give directional, not definitive, reads.

test margin impact before adopting."],"tags":["email-lifecycle","sms-marketing","win-back","automation-flows","retention","offer-design"]},{"title":"Cap SMS blasts at about two campaigns per week for most brands","summary":"Baseline around two SMS campaigns weekly, reserving higher frequency for launch-heavy or aggressive-acquisition brands with big lists.","use_when":"Setting the SMS campaign (blast) calendar and frequency for your store.","steps":["Start with a baseline of about two SMS campaigns per week for a typical brand. Send at least one per week at minimum.","For aggressive-acquisition brands spending heavily (source cites Grain's), sending an SMS every single day to people who've never bought is acceptable if you have a large list and lots of news.","Ease off for existing buyers: for one-time-purchase or subscription brands, reduce frequency to buyers, and the source says don't text active subscribers at all.","During major sale pushes you can increase to daily or even two-a-day (source references a 9-figure brand's calendar), then return to baseline after the push.","Don't force sends: the source prefers saving SMS for big announcements to avoid unsubscribes — 'do not force out SMS if you don't have to.'"],"caveats":["Frequency recommendations are the presenter's opinion and depend on list size, brand news and consent.","Buyer-vs-non-buyer cuts are specific to a sub/large-brand context."],"tags":["email-lifecycle","sms-marketing","campaign-strategy","sending-frequency","unsubscribe-management","subscription"]},{"title":"Plan an SMS campaign calendar around high-urgency events","summary":"Fill the SMS calendar with launches, restocks, time-boxed sales and timely trend/drop alerts — not evergreen nurture.","use_when":"Building the monthly SMS campaign calendar and choosing which messages to send.","steps":["Anchor sends to genuinely urgent, timely events: product launches, back-in-stock/restock alerts, flash sales, private events, insider news, and time-boxed 'selling fast this week' trend alerts.","For a launch, send the announcement, then a reminder a couple days later (source example: sent on the 4th, reminder on the 6th).","Use SMS-exclusive flash sales — the source highlights exclusive-to-list offers as especially effective.","You can relabel messages with urgency even when literal urgency is absent (e.g., frame a past collection as a 'restock,' or a product as 'running low') because restocks perform well — but note the source's caution that non-urgent nurture performed worst and drove more unsubscribes.","Example: a brand sent just five SMS in a month (pre-order collection, list-exclusive free-item offer, framed restock, reminder, launch) and reports >$100k and 16% of total store revenue — showing a lean, intentional calendar can perform."],"caveats":["This revenue example is a single case, not a benchmark.","Framing messages as 'restock' or 'running low' when untrue is the source's tactic; consider trust and advertising-standards implications before using."],"tags":["email-lifecycle","sms-marketing","campaign-strategy","launch-planning","urgency","flash-sale"]},{"title":"Broadcast SMS to the full list with a tight exclusion list","summary":"Default to sending SMS to all subscribers and only suppress chronically unengaged numbers, cleaning monthly — deep engagement segmentation leaves money on the table.","use_when":"Segmenting your SMS list for campaign sends and deciding send exclusions.","steps":["Send to all SMS subscribers rather than narrow engaged segments. The source notes people who never click a text still purchase (they see the message and go to the site directly).","Maintain a simple exclusion list: exclude a contact only after they've received ~15 texts with zero clicks ever.","Also exclude anyone you've bought from in ways that make them a poor target (e.g., don't text active subscribers on a subscription).","Clean the list about monthly to control cost, since SMS is expensive per send.","For big announcements (e.g., a New Year's Eve sale), send to the entire list with no exclusions.","Don't 'get too cute' building engaged segments — the source reports broadcasting usually makes the most money."],"caveats":["'15 texts with zero clicks' is a source heuristic, not a tested threshold.","Platform automation may handle exclusion lists differently; verify your setup."],"tags":["email-lifecycle","sms-marketing","segmentation","list-hygiene","campaign-strategy","cost-management"]},{"title":"Test delays, offers and images before scaling SMS","summary":"Validate timing, offer and image choices with A/B tests and your own brand context rather than copying a template wholesale.","use_when":"Deciding what to change or expand once your core SMS flows and campaigns are running.","steps":["Test message timing/delays (welcome day spacing, abandonment send windows, win-back trigger).","Test offers: whether a discount changes behavior, and how deep, before adding them to flows (source found no marginal lift from extra SMS discounts).","A/B test including images versus not in flows and campaigns, tracking net profit (revenue minus send cost) rather than revenue alone.","Keep the tests attached to the core flows the source says drive most revenue; add complexity only after the basics are measured.","Expect results to be brand-specific: the source explicitly says this isn't a copy-exactly recipe and cites running daily SMS or intricate flows for some brands."],"caveats":["Source advises treating its structure as a starting point, not scripture; verify with your own data.","Small-sample tests give directional, not definitive, reads."],"tags":["email-lifecycle","sms-marketing","experiment-design","conversion-optimization","abandoned-cart","measurement"]}]}

Topics. SMS marketing / Developing a profitable SMS marketing strategy by treating the channel as a high-urgency, low-frequency communication medium rather than a nurture channel. Managing the technical costs of SMS (e.g., keeping character counts under 160, limiting emojis, and evaluating the ROI of expensive MMS image sends). Establishing core automated SMS flows, including a rapid Welcome sequence, strict single-message abandonment flows (Site, Browse, Cart, Checkout) due to compliance regulations, and precisely timed post-purchase replenishment/win-back messages. list growth / Optimizing pop-up forms to capture SMS subscribers at a high rate (e.g., aiming for 15%+ opt-in rates). Utilizing interactive quiz formats or micro-commitments on platforms like Alia before requesting contact information. Maximizing phone number capture by using action-oriented copy such as "Finish signing up with text to activate your discount" rather than generic prompts like "Sign up for texts." campaign strategy / Structuring SMS campaign blasts for maximum impact and minimal unsubscribe rates. Recommending a baseline frequency of two campaigns per week for standard brands, strictly reserving SMS for high-urgency events such as product launches, back-in-stock alerts, and flash sales rather than general nurture content. Simplifying segmentation by broadcasting to the entire subscriber list while only suppressing chronically unengaged users (e.g., users who have received 15+ texts with zero clicks).

Look for. The recommended SMS platform strategy: consolidate SMS and email within the same platform (e.g., Klaviyo, Omnisend) for ease of management. The technical constraints of SMS costs: keeping messages under 160 characters and recognizing that MMS (image) messages cost roughly three times more than standard SMS. The recommended SMS campaign frequency: typically two campaigns per week, strictly reserved for high-urgency announcements. The compliance rule for abandonment flows: sending only one SMS message per abandonment event (within 48 hours).

Skip. Promotional pitches for the Well Copy agency, booking a call, or downloading the free SMS swipe file doc.

Scope mix. Almost all baseline.

Volume. 10 to 15.
